title: How Much Do Permanent Outdoor Lights Cost in Canada?
metaTitle: Permanent Outdoor Lights Cost Canada (2026 Guide)
metaDescription: What permanent outdoor lights cost in Canada in 2026: DIY kit prices by home size, installed price per linear foot, and the factors that move your total.
excerpt: A straight-talking 2026 breakdown of what permanent outdoor lights actually cost in Canada, whether you buy a DIY kit and install it yourself or hire a professional crew.
heroAlt: Two-storey Canadian home with permanent LED soffit track lights installed along the roofline
keyTakeaways: A DIY permanent LED kit for an average Canadian home runs roughly $1,200-$3,000 CAD depending on how many linear feet you need to cover.
Professional installation typically adds $8-$18 per linear foot on top of, or bundled with, the hardware, so a fully installed system commonly lands around $3,500-$8,000+ CAD.
The single biggest cost driver is linear footage of roofline, followed by home height, soffit access, and how many separate runs (power injections) your layout needs.
Buying parts and kits directly removes the biggest markup, which is why DIY can cut total cost by roughly half versus a turnkey install.
One-time permanent lighting usually pays for itself within a few seasons compared to buying temporary lights plus paying for hang-and-remove each year.

body.text: Permanent outdoor lights (also called permanent holiday lights, soffit track lights, or architectural roofline lighting) are individually addressable RGBW LED pucks recessed into an aluminum track that mounts under your soffit or along your fascia. Once installed they stay up year-round, controlled from your phone, and can produce warm white for everyday use, colour scenes for holidays, or dynamic effects for game nights. The obvious question before you commit is the honest one: what does this actually cost in Canada in 2026? Below we break down real, defensible CAD ranges for both routes: buying a DIY kit and installing it yourself, or having it professionally installed.
The two ways to buy, and why prices differ so much

Almost every quote you will see falls into one of two buckets. A DIY kit is the hardware only: the LED pucks, aluminum track, a WiFi controller, a power supply, connectors and mounting screws, shipped to your door for you to install on a weekend. A professional install is that same class of hardware plus labour, ladders, layout planning, wiring, and cleanup, priced by the linear foot and installed by a crew. The gap between the two is almost entirely labour and the installer's hardware markup, which is why DIY typically costs about half of a turnkey job for the same size of home.

Rule of thumb: measure your roofline in linear feet first. Everything else about pricing, from kit size to an installed quote, keys off that one number. Most two-storey Canadian homes land somewhere between 120 and 200 linear feet of coverable roofline.
DIY kit pricing by home size (2026 CAD)

Our DIY kits are sold as complete LED Housing Packages sized by linear footage, so you buy roughly the length you need and add a little margin for corners and offcuts. As a defensible market range across Canadian sellers, expect the following for a complete kit including pucks, track, controller and power supply:

items: 50 ft kit (small bungalow front, garage, or a single feature elevation): roughly $700-$1,200 CAD
100 ft kit (typical single-storey home or a modest two-storey front): roughly $1,200-$1,900 CAD
150 ft kit (average two-storey home, front plus partial sides): roughly $1,800-$2,600 CAD
200 ft kit (larger two-storey, wraparound coverage): roughly $2,300-$3,300 CAD

body.text: Those ranges reflect complete, warrantied kits rather than bargain-bin strip lights. Cheaper spools of generic LED tape exist, but they are not the same product: they lack individually addressable pucks, weather-rated aluminum housing, and the controllers that make year-round Canadian outdoor use reliable. You can compare exact current kit prices on our kit sizes page and see what is in each package.
Buying individual parts instead of a full kit

If you are extending an existing run, replacing a component, or building a non-standard layout, buying parts individually is often the smarter spend. As a guide to typical Canadian parts pricing in 2026:

items: 12V RGBW LED pucks: usually sold per point or in strings; budget a few dollars per point, with pucks making up the bulk of any kit's cost
Aluminum track (available in four soffit colours to blend in): commonly priced per foot or per length
WiFi 4-channel controller: roughly $60-$130 CAD depending on channel count and features
Power supply (60W to 300W): roughly $40-$140 CAD, sized to the number of pucks on the circuit
Connectors, power-injection cables and amplifiers: a few dollars to ~$40 each, needed on longer runs to keep colour and brightness even
Soffit screws and mounting hardware: a small per-pack cost

body.text: The reason we call out power injection and amplifiers is that they are the parts most first-timers forget. Long single runs lose voltage toward the far end, which shows up as dimming or colour shift. Injecting power partway along the run, or adding an amplifier, fixes it. You can browse every component on the shop page and match colours and wattages to your layout.
Professional installation pricing (2026 CAD)

If you would rather not be on a ladder, professional installation is priced per linear foot installed. Across the Canadian market in 2026, installed pricing generally falls between $8 and $18 per linear foot, hardware included, depending on your region, home height, and the installer. That means a fully installed system on an average home usually works out to something like this:

items: Smaller home, ~75-100 ft installed: roughly $1,500-$3,000 CAD
Average two-storey, ~150 ft installed: roughly $3,000-$5,500 CAD
Larger home with wraparound coverage, 200+ ft: roughly $5,000-$8,000+ CAD

If you are outside that area, the DIY kit ships Canada-wide and is designed to be installed with basic tools in a weekend. You can request a local quote on the installation page.
What actually drives your cost
Two homes on the same street can get very different quotes. Here is what moves the number, roughly in order of impact:

items: Linear footage: the number one factor for both DIY and installed pricing, because it sets how many pucks and how much track you need.
Home height and access: two- and three-storey homes, steep rooflines, or hard-to-reach peaks add labour time and safety equipment to an installed quote.
Number of runs and power injections: complex layouts with several separate sections need extra controllers, injections, or amplifiers.
Soffit condition and colour matching: choosing a track colour to match your soffit is free, but damaged or unusually deep soffits can add labour.
Controller and feature level: single-zone versus multi-zone control and app features nudge the hardware price.
Region and season: installer rates vary by market, and booking in the busy autumn run-up to the holidays can cost more than the off-season.

body.text: Watch out for quotes priced only 'per home' with no linear-foot breakdown. Ask for the footage and the per-foot rate so you can compare apples to apples, and confirm the warranty length and whether returns are supported.
Is permanent lighting worth it versus temporary lights?

Permanent lighting is a larger one-time cost, but it replaces a recurring one. Buying and replacing temporary light strings, plus paying a service to hang and remove them each year, adds up quickly. In many Canadian markets a professional hang-and-remove alone runs several hundred dollars every season, before you count damaged strings and storage. A permanent system removes that annual bill and gives you everyday architectural lighting, holiday colour, and security lighting from a single install. For most homeowners the payback lands within a few seasons, and DIY shortens that further by removing labour cost entirely.
So, what should you budget?

For a realistic 2026 plan: if you are handy and want the best value, budget roughly $1,200-$3,000 CAD for a complete DIY kit sized to your home, with free shipping on orders over $500 and a 5-year warranty behind the hardware. If you would rather have it installed and you are in the London, Woodstock, or Kitchener-Waterloo area, budget around $8-$18 per linear foot installed, which for most homes means roughly $3,500-$8,000. Either way, start by measuring your roofline: that single number tells you which kit size to look at and gives any installer the basis for an honest quote. When you are ready, compare the kit sizes to find your fit, pick up any individual parts you need from the shop, or book a local installation if you would like our crew to handle it.
